title: How To Improve Attentiveness In 5 Minutes
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This article proposes a five-minute exercise break as a quick fix when students become restless and inattentive partway through the school day. Linsin explains that pushing through or lecturing rarely works because attention naturally wanes, and the better response is to get students moving. He offers ten specific, teacher-led exercises - from air swimming and jumping jacks to desk push-ups, yoga poses, and burpees - that require no equipment and can be done in the classroom. He recommends pairing the movement with music to further sharpen focus and mood, and suggests scheduling two breaks a day (morning and afternoon) so students anticipate and look forward to them rather than needing them as an emergency measure. A brief safety note reminds teachers to stay attentive to individual students' physical limitations.
points: Restlessness and inattentiveness partway through the day are best solved with movement, not more talk or discipline.
Ten no-equipment exercises (air swimming, jumping jacks, run intervals, desk push-ups, yoga poses, circles, no-weight gym moves, burpees, twists) can be led in five minutes.
Pairing exercise with music enhances the mental-clarity and mood benefits of the break.
Scheduling breaks proactively (morning and afternoon) is more effective than waiting until students are already off task.
quotes: Your students are chatty and distracted. Their heads are on a swivel. They’re squirming in their seats. Only the most dedicated appear to be following along.
The problem with these methods is that they’re unlikely to work for more than a few minutes. The fact is, regardless of how old they are, your students can only sit and attend for so long.
An exercise break is an easy and effective strategy that also happens to be backed by science.
After just five minutes of moderate exercise, your students will be refreshed, recharged, and ready to learn.
When combined with exercise, music clears the mind and improves mental performance.
I’ve found that if you schedule your exercise breaks–once in the morning and once in the afternoon–your students will look forward to them.
